solution.concept_anchor: Adinath's first sermon location and Hindu textual reference

statement_analysis.statement: According to Shvetambara Jain tradition, Adinath (Rishabhanatha) delivered his first sermon (samavasarana) on Shatrunjaya Hill, which is the doctrinal basis for the hill's supreme sanctity in Shvetambara Jainism.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the foundational narrative establishing Shatrunjaya's sacred status — Adinath's samavasarana on this hill is the theological anchor of the entire Palitana pilgrimage tradition.

statement_analysis.statement: Rishabhanatha is described in the Rigveda as a divine teacher, making him the only Tirthankara with a direct mention in the Vedic corpus itself.
statement_analysis.reason: Rishabhanatha is mentioned in the Bhagavata Purana and in early Shaiva texts — but his mention in the Rigveda specifically is not a well-established scholarly consensus. Additionally, the 'only Tirthankara' qualifier is an over-extension. This statement contains a conflation of different text traditions.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who have read about Rishabhanatha's cross-religious textual mentions may accept Statement 2 because they know he is referenced in Hindu texts, without distinguishing between 'Rigveda' and 'Bhagavata Purana' as specific texts.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Adinath's samavasarana on Shatrunjaya is the established Shvetambara doctrinal narrative — correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: 'Described in the Rigveda' — Rishabhanatha's established cross-textual reference is the Bhagavata Purana, not the Rigveda. Attributing a specific Puranic reference to the Rigveda is a text-swap error. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap in Statement 2 substitutes 'Bhagavata Purana' (the correct text) with 'Rigveda.' Students who know Rishabhanatha has cross-religious textual mentions in Hindu literature may accept this claim without distinguishing between Vedic and Puranic literature. The Bhagavata Purana (Book 5) contains a detailed account of Rishabha/Rishabhanatha — this is the correct text. The Rigveda reference is an entity-swap that exploits imprecise memory of which Hindu text contains the cross-reference.
solution.final_explanation:
Cross-textual references to Jain Tirthankaras in Hindu literature are a tested dimension of comparative religion in UPSC, requiring precision about which specific texts contain these references.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Shvetambara tradition holds that Adinath delivered his divine assembly (samavasarana) on Shatrunjaya Hill. This narrative is the theological foundation of Palitana's pre-eminent status — pilgrimage to this spot is understood as following in the footsteps of the first Tirthankara's enlightened teaching.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Rishabhanatha's cross-religious textual presence is in the Bhagavata Purana (Canto 5), not the Rigveda. The Rigveda attribution is factually incorrect. Additionally, the qualifier 'only Tirthankara with a direct Vedic mention' introduces an unverifiable absolute claim.

Value Addition:
• The Bhagavata Purana's account of Rishabha (Book 5) portrays him as an avatar of Vishnu — demonstrating the extent of Hindu-Jain cultural syncretism.
• The Rigveda does mention 'Rishabha' in a different context (as a bull/powerful one) but this is not the same as describing the Jain Tirthankara.
• Neminatha (22nd Tirthankara) is associated with Krishna's lineage in both Jain and Hindu traditions — another cross-religious textual connection.

solution.concept_anchor: UNESCO tentative list criteria — OUV criteria for Palitana nomination
solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know UNESCO World Heritage Sites are assessed for Outstanding Universal Value may select (d) — criterion (iii) alone — knowing it covers living traditions, but the question tests the specific combination of criteria under which the Palitana nomination was filed.
elimination_logic: The Palitana nomination was filed under OUV criteria (i), (ii), and (vi).
Criterion (i) relates to masterpieces of human creative genius — the architectural excellence of 900+ temples applies.
Criterion (ii) relates to interchange of human values — Palitana's role in developing Nagara-Jain architectural tradition.
Criterion (vi) relates to direct association with living traditions, beliefs, events of outstanding universal significance — the Jain pilgrimage tradition.
Eliminate (a): criteria (iii) and (iv) relate to civilisation/landscape — not the primary basis for Palitana's nomination.
Eliminate (c): criteria (vii) and (x) are natural heritage criteria — entirely inapplicable.
Eliminate (d): criterion (iii) alone (civilisation testimony) undersells the nomination — (i), (ii), (vi) is the correct set.
Confirm (b): OUV criteria (i), (ii), and (vi) match the documented basis for Palitana's 2014 tentative list nomination.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap tests whether students know the specific criteria combination rather than just knowing that Palitana was nominated. Option (d) isolates criterion (vi) — which is the most intuitive choice for a pilgrimage site (living traditions) — but the nomination includes criteria (i) (architectural masterpiece) and (ii) (interchange of values) as well. A student who knows criterion (vi) is relevant but hasn't retained the full set will over-restrict the answer to (d).
solution.final_explanation:
UNESCO World Heritage nominations are filed under specific Outstanding Universal Value (OUV) criteria numbered (i) through (x), with (i)-(vi) covering cultural heritage and (vii)-(x) covering natural heritage.

Applicable scenario: A heritage expert recommending which criteria to invoke for Palitana's nomination must identify the combination that best captures the site's multi-dimensional significance.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Criteria (iii) (civilisation testimony) and (iv) (architectural typology) are individually relevant but are not the primary criteria under which Palitana's nomination was filed.
• Option (b) — Correct: Criteria (i) (masterpiece of creative genius — architectural excellence of 900+ temples), (ii) (interchange of human values — development of Maru-Gurjara/Nagara-Jain tradition), and (vi) (direct association with living traditions and beliefs of outstanding significance — the Shvetambara Jain pilgrimage tradition) are the documented basis for the 2014 tentative list submission.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Criteria (vii) and (x) are natural heritage criteria — these apply to natural beauty and biodiversity, not cultural monuments.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Criterion (vi) alone understates the architectural and cultural exchange dimensions of the nomination.

Value Addition:
• Champaner-Pavagadh (inscribed 2004) was filed under criteria (iii) and (iv) — compare with Palitana's (i), (ii), (vi).
• The 10 UNESCO OUV criteria are tested in UPSC through differentiation between cultural (i–vi) and natural (vii–x) categories.
• India has 42 UNESCO World Heritage Sites as of 2024 — 34 cultural, 7 natural, 1 mixed.

solution.concept_anchor: Maru-Gurjara style temples — geographic and dynastic identification
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know Somnath is a Solanki-period temple and is in Gujarat may pair it with Maru-Gurjara style, not realising it was rebuilt multiple times and is not a primary example of the architectural style — whereas Modhera is the textbook Maru-Gurjara Sun Temple example.
elimination_logic: Examine pair (a): Modhera Sun Temple (Hindu) in Mehsana district, Gujarat — built during Solanki period — is the textbook example of Maru-Gurjara (Nagara regional variant) architecture. This pairing is correct.
Examine pair (b): Dilwara temples are in Sirohi district, Rajasthan (at Mt. Abu) — not in Gujarat. The geographic assignment is wrong.

Examine pair (c): Somnath has been rebuilt multiple times (12 destructions and reconstructions) — its current structure is a 20th-century reconstruction in Chalukya style, not a primary example of original Solanki Maru-Gurjara architecture.
Examine pair (d): Rani-ki-Vav is in Patan, Gujarat — but it is a stepwell (vav), not a temple — pairing it with 'Nagara temple architecture' is incorrect.
Confirm (a): Modhera Sun Temple is the correctly matched pair.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap in pair (b) moves Dilwara from its correct location (Mt. Abu, Sirohi district, Rajasthan) to Gujarat — students who know Dilwara is a major Jain site and that both Palitana and Dilwara are in the same pilgrimage circuit may assume both are in Gujarat. The Somnath trap (c) exploits students' knowledge that Somnath is a famous Solanki-period temple in Gujarat, but the current structure is not original Solanki Maru-Gurjara architecture.
solution.final_explanation:
The Maru-Gurjara style is the defining regional architectural vocabulary of the Solanki period in Gujarat and Rajasthan — identifying its exemplary monuments requires both geographic and stylistic precision.

• Option (a) — Correct: The Modhera Sun Temple in Mehsana district, Gujarat (early 11th century, Solanki period) is the paradigmatic example of Maru-Gurjara architecture — a Nagara regional variant with distinctive decorative programmes, a stepped tank (Surya Kund), and a main shrine with assembly hall.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Dilwara temples are located on Mount Abu in Sirohi district, Rajasthan — not in Gujarat. This is a geographic-swap error.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Somnath (Prabhas Patan, Gujarat) has been rebuilt 12 times — the current temple was reconstructed in 1951. It cannot be cited as a primary example of original Solanki Maru-Gurjara architecture.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Rani-ki-Vav (Patan, Gujarat) is a UNESCO-inscribed stepped well (vav), not a temple. Pairing it with 'Nagara temple architecture' is categorically incorrect.

Value Addition:
• Modhera Sun Temple features a Surya Kund (stepped tank with 108 shrines) — a unique integration of water architecture and temple complex.
• Rani-ki-Vav was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014.
• Solanki-period monuments also include Siddhapur (Rudra Mahalaya) — a partially destroyed Solanki temple complex.

statement_analysis.statement: Shravanabelagola in Karnataka is a Digambara Jain pilgrimage site famous for the monolithic statue of Bahubali (Gommateshvara), which is the largest monolithic statue in the world.
statement_analysis.reason: The Bahubali statue at Shravanabelagola (57.5 feet) is not the largest monolithic statue in the world — that distinction belongs to much larger modern statues. However, it IS among the tallest monolithic freestanding statues from the medieval period. The claim 'largest in the world' is an over-extension.

statement_analysis.statement: Mudabidri in Karnataka, like Shravanabelagola, is a Digambara Jain site — making Karnataka a significant centre for Digambara Jain heritage, distinct from the Shvetambara-dominated Gujarat-Rajasthan region.
statement_analysis.reason: Both Shravanabelagola and Mudabidri are Digambara sites in Karnataka — the geographic distinction between Digambara (Karnataka) and Shvetambara (Gujarat-Rajasthan) sacred circuits is a standard differentiation point.

statement_analysis.statement: The concept of 'tirtha' in Jain tradition refers not only to physical pilgrimage sites but also to the four-fold community (sangha) of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen — reflecting a broader doctrinal meaning.
statement_analysis.reason: In Jain philosophy, 'tirtha' has a dual meaning — it refers both to the physical sacred site and, more fundamentally, to the four-fold sangha (chaturvidha sangha) which is itself considered a tirtha because it enables spiritual crossing (tara/tirtha = crossing over).

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who correctly doubt Statement 1 (the 'world's largest' claim is over-extended) but are uncertain about Statement 3's philosophical dimension (tirtha as sangha) may hedge and select only Statement 2, choosing option (c) — 2 only — instead of the correct (d) — 2 and 3.
elimination_logic: Examine Statement 1: 'largest monolithic statue in the world' — Bahubali at Shravanabelagola is 57.5 feet. Modern statues (e.g., Spring Temple Buddha at 420 feet) are far larger. The 'largest in the world' claim is incorrect.
Verify Statement 2: Mudabidri is a Digambara site in Karnataka — paired with Shravanabelagola, this correctly describes the Karnataka-Digambara axis. Correct.

Statements 2 and 3 are correct — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap in Statement 1 takes a real and famous fact (Bahubali's monolithic statue at Shravanabelagola is remarkable and historically significant) and over-extends it with 'largest in the world.' The statue is among the tallest freestanding medieval monolithic statues globally, but modern statues surpass it in height. Students who have memorised 'Shravanabelagola — tallest monolithic statue' may accept the over-extended claim. Statement 3's philosophical dimension about tirtha as sangha is a less-tested fact that many students may doubt, making them under-count the correct statements.
solution.final_explanation:
Jain sacred geography requires distinguishing sectarian affiliations, geographic clusters, and the theological depth of pilgrimage concepts.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Gommateshvara (Bahubali) statue at Shravanabelagola stands approximately 57.5 feet tall — a significant medieval monument, but not the world's largest monolithic statue. The 'world's largest' claim is an over-extension that makes the statement factually incorrect.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Mudabidri (Dakshina Kannada district, Karnataka) is a Digambara site containing the 'Jain Kashi' — an important pilgrimage town with 18 Jain basadis (temples). Together with Shravanabelagola, it defines Karnataka as the Digambara heartland.
• Statement 3 — Correct: 'Tirtha' in Jain philosophy has a dual doctrinal meaning — the physical place of pilgrimage AND the chaturvidha sangha (four-fold community: sadhus, sadhvis, shravaks, shravikas). This dual meaning is fundamental to Jain soteriology.

Value Addition:
• The Mahamastakabhisheka at Shravanabelagola (Bahubali anointing) occurs every 12 years — one of the largest Jain religious gatherings.
• Mudabidri is known as 'Jain Kashi' — its Thousand Pillar Temple (Tribhuvana Tilaka Chudamani) is a celebrated Digambara monument.
• The chaturvidha sangha concept is central to both Shvetambara and Digambara traditions, though the definition of 'monk' differs between them.

solution.concept_anchor: Palitana pilgrimage infrastructure — steps, tuks, Navanu Yatra, overnight restriction

statement_analysis.statement: The Palitana temple complex is often described as a 'city of temples' because its 900+ shrines are organized into 9 tuks (enclosures), each managed by a distinct Jain merchant community.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the standard description — 900+ temples in 9 tuks, each under distinct community management, creating the 'city of temples' designation.

statement_analysis.statement: The approximately 3,800 stone steps to the summit represent not just a physical path but a ritual discipline — each step conceived as a unit of spiritual progress in the Jain tradition.
statement_analysis.reason: The steps are intentionally designed as a ritual element — the physical ascent is a metaphor for spiritual liberation (moksha), making the count of steps a theologically significant architectural feature.

statement_analysis.statement: The prohibition on overnight stay atop Shatrunjaya applies only during the Paryushana festival period, when the hill's ritual sanctity is considered heightened above its normal condition.
statement_analysis.reason: The overnight stay prohibition is a permanent, year-round doctrinal rule — not restricted to the Paryushana period. It applies without exception throughout the year.

statement_analysis.statement: The 'Navanu Yatra' practice — completing 99 pilgrimage ascents of Shatrunjaya — has significant social and economic implications, as wealthy Jain patrons historically funded infrastructure (dharamshalas, water points) along the pilgrimage route.
statement_analysis.reason: The merit-accumulation system of Navanu Yatra had direct social-economic effects — patrons who undertook or funded multiple yatras also funded supporting infrastructure, linking religious merit with philanthropic construction.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who correctly identify Statements 1, 2, and 4 as correct but accept Statement 3's 'Paryushana restriction' as plausible (because Paryushana IS the holiest period) will count all four as correct and select (d).
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: 900+ temples in 9 tuks, community-managed — standard fact, correct.
Verify Statement 2: 3,800 steps as ritual discipline and moksha metaphor — correct.
Examine Statement 3 carefully: 'only during Paryushana' — the overnight ban is ABSOLUTE and year-round, not season-specific. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 4: Navanu Yatra's social-economic implications (funding dharamshalas) — correct.
Three statements correct (1, 2, 4) — select (c) Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap in Statement 3 combines two real facts — the overnight prohibition (true) and the heightened sanctity during Paryushana (true) — and incorrectly links them by suggesting the prohibition applies only during Paryushana. Students who know Paryushana is the most sacred Jain period may accept the conditional restriction as a reasonable doctrinal refinement. The absolute nature of the prohibition (year-round, no exceptions) is the precise knowledge required to flag Statement 3 as incorrect.
solution.final_explanation:
Multiple architectural, ritual, and social dimensions of Palitana converge in this question — each statement tests a different factual layer.

• Statement 1 — Correct: 900+ temples in 9 tuks under distinct community management is the defining organisational feature of Palitana — the basis for its 'city of temples' designation.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The 3,800+ steps are architecturally and theologically deliberate — physical effort as spiritual discipline, each step a ritual act on the path toward moksha.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The overnight stay prohibition is absolute and year-round — it is not a seasonal restriction tied to Paryushana. The rule reflects the belief that the hill's sacred nature must remain uncontaminated by sleep and bodily activities at all times.
• Statement 4 — Correct: The Navanu Yatra (99 pilgrimages) created an institutional cycle of merit-accumulation and philanthropic investment — wealthy merchants funded dharamshalas, water stations, and rest facilities, creating the integrated pilgrimage infrastructure visible today.

Value Addition:
• Paryushana (Shvetambara) / Paryushana Parva (Digambara: Das Lakshana) — the most sacred festival in the Jain calendar, involving fasting, confession, and forgiveness rituals.
• The Anandji Kalyanji Trust oversees the maintenance of the pilgrimage infrastructure funded historically by Seth patronage.
• Palki (palanquin) carriers who assist elderly pilgrims up the 3,800 steps are an intangible heritage community whose livelihood depends on the pilgrimage economy.

solution.concept_anchor: Mahmud Begada's destruction of Palitana — 1479 CE
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know Muzaffar Shah also destroyed temples at Palitana and who conflate the two Gujarat Sultanate rulers may assign the 1479 CE destruction to Muzaffar Shah rather than Mahmud Begada.
elimination_logic: The question asks who is specifically attributed with the 1479 CE destruction at Palitana.
Eliminate (a): Alauddin Khilji is associated with attacks on Gujarat in 1299 CE — much earlier, and not the 1479 CE event.
Eliminate (c): Muzaffar Shah is associated with a SEPARATE destruction event — the 1479 CE specific attribution belongs to Mahmud Begada.
Eliminate (d): Sher Shah Suri operated primarily in the 1540s in North India — not a Gujarat Sultanate ruler associated with Palitana.
Confirm (b): Mahmud Begada (Sultan of Gujarat, r. 1459–1511 CE) is specifically attributed with the destruction of Palitana temples in 1479 CE.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap works because both Mahmud Begada and Muzaffar Shah were Gujarat Sultanate rulers who affected Jain temple sites. Students who know 'a Gujarat Sultan destroyed Palitana' but haven't retained which specific Sultan did so at which specific date will confuse the two. Mahmud Begada (1479 CE) and Muzaffar Shah are both real figures in Palitana's destruction history — the question tests whether students have mapped the specific year to the specific ruler.
solution.final_explanation:
Palitana's medieval history involves multiple episodes of destruction at the hands of Gujarat Sultanate rulers, and distinguishing between them requires ruler-specific knowledge.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Alauddin Khilji raided Gujarat in 1299 CE but is not the ruler associated with the 1479 CE Palitana destruction.
• Option (b) — Correct: Mahmud Begada (ruled Gujarat 1459–1511 CE) is specifically attributed with the destruction of the Palitana temples in 1479 CE. He was also known for converting and demolishing several Hindu and Jain temples across Gujarat.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Muzaffar Shah (there were two Muzaffar Shahs of Gujarat) is associated with a different destruction episode — conflating him with the 1479 CE event is the primary trap.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Sher Shah Suri (Suri dynasty, North India, 1540s) has no documented role in Palitana's destruction history.

Value Addition:
• Mahmud Begada was the most powerful Sultan of the Gujarat Sultanate — he also conquered Junagadh (Girnar) and Pavagadh.
• The Anandji Kalyanji Trust and predecessor Seth communities undertook reconstruction after the 1479 CE destruction.
• The 1618 CE reconstruction falls under Jahangir's Mughal period — a chronological precision often tested.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 26 religious management vs. state regulatory power — Palitana context

statement_analysis.statement: Article 26 of the Constitution protects the right of religious denominations to establish and manage religious institutions — a provision under which the Anandji Kalyanji Trust's administrative autonomy over Palitana's temples is constitutionally protected.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 26 guarantees every religious denomination the right to manage its own affairs in matters of religion and to maintain institutions for religious purposes — the Trust's autonomy is directly protected under this provision.

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court's interpretation of Article 26 holds that the state can regulate ALL activities of a religious institution, including purely spiritual practices, provided the regulation serves a public purpose.
statement_analysis.reason: The Supreme Court (Shirur Mutt case and subsequent judgments) has specifically held that Article 26's protection of 'affairs of religion' extends to purely spiritual practices, which the state CANNOT regulate — the state's regulatory power under Article 26 is limited to the secular (non-religious) activities of religious institutions.

statement_analysis.statement: The 2014 declaration of Palitana as a fully vegetarian city was issued through municipal authority powers — not through a direct exercise of Article 26 by the Jain religious community.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 26 protects religious denominations' right to manage their internal affairs — it does not give them the power to impose food laws on a civic area. The vegetarian declaration was a government municipal notification, not an Article 26 exercise.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know the state has SOME power to regulate religious institutions may incorrectly accept Statement 2's over-extension ('ALL activities including purely spiritual') and select option (b) — 1 and 3 only, doubting Statement 2 — but then incorrectly not including it.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Article 26's protection of the Trust's religious management autonomy — correct and precisely stated.

Examine Statement 2: 'ALL activities including purely spiritual practices' — the Supreme Court explicitly prohibits state regulation of purely spiritual/religious activities under Article 26. The 'ALL activities' scope-extension makes Statement 2 incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: The vegetarian declaration was issued through municipal authority, not Article 26 exercise — correct and constitutionally accurate.
Statements 1 and 3 correct; Statement 2 incorrect — select option (d): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 2 converts the Supreme Court's nuanced position ('state can regulate secular activities of religious institutions') into an absolute ('state can regulate ALL activities'). This over-extension sounds like a stronger version of a real rule and may be accepted by students who know the state has some regulatory power over religious institutions but have not retained the precise limitation — that purely spiritual/religious practices are beyond state regulatory power under Article 26.
solution.final_explanation:
The constitutional law governing religious institutions in India involves a crucial distinction between religious and secular activities — a distinction that directly applies to Palitana's administration.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 26 grants every religious denomination four rights: to establish and maintain religious institutions, to manage its own affairs in matters of religion, to own property, and to administer its property. The Anandji Kalyanji Trust's autonomy over Palitana's temples is protected under the first two of these.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Supreme Court in the Shirur Mutt case (1954) and subsequent judgments has established that the state's regulatory power under Article 26 extends only to the SECULAR activities of religious institutions (financial management, civic compliance, non-religious administration). The state CANNOT regulate purely spiritual practices or matters of religious doctrine under Article 26.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The 2014 vegetarian city declaration was issued through the State government's municipal authority under Article 243W and State municipal laws — the Jain community used Article 26 as a political argument, but the legal mechanism was municipal, not a direct invocation of Article 26.

Value Addition:
• Shirur Mutt case (1954): Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar — foundational case defining the religious vs. secular activities distinction.
• The Ratilal Panachand Gandhi v. State of Bombay (1954) further refined Article 26 protections for Jain trusts.
• Article 25(2) allows the state to regulate 'secular activities associated with religious practice' — this must be read alongside Article 26's stronger denomination-level protection.

solution.concept_anchor: Palitana vs. Dilwara — material and style comparison

statement_analysis.statement: Both Palitana and Dilwara temples use white marble as a primary building material, but Dilwara's interior marble filigree (jaali) carving is considered architecturally unparalleled, while Palitana is distinguished by the scale of its multi-temple cluster.
statement_analysis.reason: Both sites do use white marble (Palitana uses Makrana and local varieties; Dilwara uses exclusively white marble). The distinction between Dilwara's interior filigree craftsmanship and Palitana's scale-and-cluster model is accurate.

statement_analysis.statement: The Dilwara temples follow the Dravida architectural style, with characteristic pyramidal towers, which is why their interior marble carving achieves greater height and visual drama than the horizontally organised Nagara temples at Palitana.
statement_analysis.reason: Dilwara temples follow the Nagara style (Maru-Gurjara variant) — not the Dravida style. Both Dilwara and Palitana are Nagara-tradition temples. The claim about pyramidal towers and greater height due to Dravida style is entirely fabricated.

solution.strong_distractor: a — The correct answer is (a) — Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — which means option (c) in the standard format. But since this is two-statement-relationship, option (c) maps to Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect. Wait — re-checking the option mapping for this question.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Both sites use white marble — true. Dilwara's interior jaali work is unparalleled — true. Palitana is distinguished by scale/cluster — true. Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: 'Dilwara follows Dravida style with pyramidal towers' — Dilwara is unambiguously a Nagara-style complex (Maru-Gurjara variant). This is factually wrong. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — the matching option is (c): Statement 1 is correct but Statement 2 is incorrect.
Wait — correct_option should be (c). Re-check: option (a) = both correct, (b) = both incorrect, (c) = S1 correct S2 incorrect, (d) = S1 incorrect S2 correct. Correct answer = (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap in Statement 2 assigns the Dravida style (South Indian pyramid towers) to Dilwara, which is a Nagara (North Indian curvilinear spire) complex. Students who know Dravida and Nagara are two major temple styles and that they differ in tower form may accept the characterisation of Dilwara as Dravida because the interior of Dilwara's temples has extraordinary three-dimensional carved ceilings that can visually suggest greater vertical drama — but this has nothing to do with Dravida style. Both Palitana and Dilwara are firmly in the Nagara tradition.
solution.final_explanation:
Comparing Dilwara and Palitana requires knowing both their material similarities and their stylistic identity.

• Statement 1 — Correct: White marble is used at both sites, though Dilwara uses exclusively high-grade white marble while Palitana incorporates Makrana and local varieties. The distinguishing feature of each is accurately captured — Dilwara's extraordinary interior marble filigree versus Palitana's unmatched scale as a temple cluster.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Both Dilwara and Palitana are Nagara-style temples — specifically the Maru-Gurjara regional variant of the Nagara tradition. Dilwara has no pyramidal Dravida towers. The extraordinary ceiling sculptures and carved marble domes at Dilwara are a function of Nagara interior craftsmanship, not Dravida structural form.

Value Addition:
• Dilwara's Vimala Vasahi (1031 CE) is dedicated to Adinath; Luna Vasahi (1230 CE) to Neminatha — both are Maru-Gurjara Nagara structures.
• The Maru-Gurjara style is sometimes called 'Chaulukya style' after the Solanki (Chaulukya) dynasty.
• Interior marble ceilings at Dilwara are formed through subtraction (carving away solid marble) rather than mosaic addition — a technically demanding process that accounts for their extraordinary delicacy.
